Triggers.value: Difficulty breathing or feeling short of breath

Memory.value: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I have to be on guard all the time

vignette:
Kwame is a 20-year-old African American medical resident who came for treatment looking younger than he is, shoulders held tight and eyes scanning the room before he sat down. He had served in combat before entering medicine, and when he speaks about the event that still governs his days, he can only do it in jagged fragments. He remembers being with other soldiers in a built-up area after a burst of violence, the air thick with dust and smoke, trying to breathe through a chest that felt locked. He remembers sudden gunfire, then a stretch of unnatural silence so complete that it felt more dangerous than the noise. After that, the memory breaks apart. There are disconnected pieces-someone shouting, the sensation of not getting enough air, the sight of bodies and movement-but large sections are simply gone. Each time he gets close to the missing part, he feels himself forcibly pushing the memory away before it can fully come into view.

In the months afterward, what unsettled him most was not only what had happened but what it seemed to say about the world and about him. Kwame had come to believe that the basic rules he once relied on no longer held: safety could vanish without warning, silence could hide catastrophe, and violence could erupt out of nowhere. He says he no longer knows himself in the way he once did. Before, he thought of himself as focused, purposeful, and steady under pressure; now he is certain he must stay on guard at all times, as if letting that vigilance drop would be a kind of fatal mistake. That altered sense of himself shapes the way he encounters ordinary experience. If the hallway outside a patient's room falls suddenly quiet, he does not register it as calm; he feels his body tense with the conviction that danger is gathering. If he becomes short of breath climbing stairs at the hospital, the sensation is immediately loaded with the meaning that he is back in a moment when control was gone. Seeing violence in the emergency department-an injured patient brought in after an assault, security rushing toward a combative visitor-hits him with the force of confirmation that the world is exactly as ruined and unpredictable as he has come to believe.

Those beliefs also seem to govern what happens when he tries to remember. When he edges toward the worst parts of the combat experience, the effort quickly becomes bound up with the thought that the memory could undo him completely, that if he lets himself know it in full he may discover something unbearable about who he is now. The result is that he blocks it off before it is complete. He describes getting only flashes, then a blank wall. The more he experiences the memory as broken and inaccessible, the more alien he feels to himself. He is shaken by the fact that he cannot produce a coherent account of what happened, and he takes those gaps personally, as further evidence that something fundamental in him has been damaged. For Kwame, not remembering smoothly is not neutral confusion; it deepens his sense that his old assumptions and identity have been destroyed.

That fragmented remembering also keeps his triggers potent. Because the event survives in disconnected sensory pieces rather than a full narrative, a particular bodily sensation or environmental shift can feel less like a reminder and more like part of the event happening again. Breathlessness is especially difficult. During long shifts at the hospital, if he has been rushing between patients and suddenly notices he cannot catch his breath, the sensation arrives stripped of context and fused to those incomplete fragments from combat. A stretch of sudden silence at the nurses' station can have a similar effect. He becomes intensely alert, listening for what should come next, because the silence belongs to the memory even though the memory itself will not hold still long enough to be known.

Over time, this has narrowed his life at work and outside it. As a doctor, he keeps himself in constant motion, preferring noise and activity over stillness because quiet feels dangerous. He avoids lingering after violent cases in the emergency department and will hand off tasks if a patient's injuries are too close to what he can half remember. He tells himself this is simply being efficient and composed, but underneath he is trying not to set off the bodily panic, the fragments, and the conviction that he is no longer the person he was. What finally brought him to seek help was the realization that the cycle was beginning to define both his training and his sense of self. He is frightened that if this continues he will lose his future in medicine, and perhaps the last stable version of himself he still hopes can be recovered.
